title: Metrics platform
brief: Thousands of services send a stream of measurements: CPU, errors, latency. You store them, draw the dashboards and fire the alerts. The platform watching everyone else must never go down first, and one customer creating millions of new series can ruin the bill.

clarify.a: About 17 million different series, each sampled every 15 seconds. That is around 1.1 million samples every second.

clarify.q: Is it OK to lose a few seconds of measurements?
clarify.a: About a minute is fine. But alerts must keep working during problems.

clarify.q: How long do we keep data?
clarify.a: Fifteen days at full detail. Older data is summarised elsewhere.

clarify.q: What if one team creates a million new series by accident?
clarify.a: Limit new series per team so one mistake cannot hurt everyone.

notes: One ingest request batches 100 samples. Use the peak request rate and telemetry share above to estimate the batch rate.
A sample takes about 1.5 bytes after compression (approx.).

text.name: Dashboard rush
text.description: Teams open dashboards at nine. Read and report traffic rises to eight times normal while agents keep sending measurements.

debrief.headline: Nine o’clock dashboard rush: reads and reports rose eightfold.
debrief.hurt: {failed} requests failed as query traffic rose. Ingest continued on its separate path.
debrief.fix: Cache repeated dashboard queries and leave query capacity for cold misses. The ingest limiter cannot protect this separate read path.

numbers.label: Ingest batches per second at peak
Database nodes needed for writes
numbers.how: 11,200 ÷ 3,000 batches per node ≈ 4; use more for headroom (approx.)

numbers.label: Data held for 15 days, three copies
numbers.how: 1.1 M samples/s × 1.5 B × 86,400 × 15 days × 3 copies ≈ 6.4 TB (approx.)

hints: Writes are constant and huge, reads come in bursts when people open dashboards. Do they need the same machines?
Buffer incoming data in an event stream, spread series over many database nodes (shards), and cache repeated dashboard reads.
Missing measurements cannot establish health. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: Ingest and query are separate paths that share only the time-series store. Ingest is buffered by a stream so a slow database cannot cause drops. Series are spread across shards. Queries are cached because dashboards repeat. A per-team limit stops runaway series.

designs.name: Buffered ingest, sharded store, cached queries
designs.why: Distributors accept data quickly, the stream holds it, and processors write it in batches to shards in three zones. Dashboards are served by query servers with a cache, so nine o'clock dashboards do not hurt ingestion.

tradeoffs: The stream adds a few seconds before data is queryable, but protects against drops when the database stalls.
More shards means more write capacity and more copies of the cluster to run. Choosing the shard key matters.
Query caching makes busy dashboards cheap but may show data up to a minute old.
Per-team limits stop runaway series, but a limit set too low silently drops real data from a busy team.
editorial.realWorld: Large metrics clusters ingest tens of millions of samples a second across hundreds of nodes. Cost scales with the number of distinct series more than with the sample rate (approx.).

correctness.prompt: Metrics platform: which invariant does this trace protect, and what failure would break it?
correctness.discussion: Isolate tenants and bound label cardinality while preserving useful alerts. Series state can exhaust memory even at a moderate sample rate. Isolation needs separate budgets and visible failure, not silent gaps. Missing measurements cannot establish health.

fields.label: Step 1. Tenant T adds a unique request id label to every sample. What is bounded?
options: Active series creation and per-tenant resource budgets
fields.explanation: Series state can exhaust memory even at a moderate sample rate.

fields.label: Step 2. T hits its limit during another tenant’s incident. What remains usable?
options: A shared queue that T may fill indefinitely
Other tenants’ ingestion and queries, with explicit rejection feedback to T
fields.explanation: Isolation needs separate budgets and visible failure, not silent gaps.

fields.label: Step 3. An alert evaluation misses its data freshness target. What should it report?
options: Stale or unknown evaluation with ingestion lag evidence
Healthy because no fresh failures were found

correctness.responsibility: Isolate tenants and bound label cardinality while preserving useful alerts.
correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.

twist.brief: Demand has settled at about 3,500 requests/s. The new monthly ceiling is $34,974. The original burst reserve now competes with the operating budget. Decide which reserve to keep, then test its failure headroom. All data and recovery promises still apply.

design.name: Smaller workload, measured reserve
design.why: Reduce the paid floor for the quieter workload, preserving the required copies and recovery settings. This design was checked through the full event day.
